articles.title: South Korea-Tanzania Cooperation Spearheads Infrastructure Autonomy Era - The Tanzania Times
articles.summary: South Korea-Tanzania Cooperation Spearheads Infrastructure Autonomy Era  The Tanzania Times
articles.full_text:
In an assertive step toward executing its landmark Development Vision 2050, Tanzania is orchestrating a historic, high-impact overhaul of its national transportation and trade architecture.
This is through a deeply integrated bilateral alliance with the Republic of Korea, led by its state-owned rail giant, Korea Railroad Corporation (KORAIL).
Positioned far beyond the traditional role of a standard technical advisor, South Korea—through KORAIL—has established itself as the indispensable architect, chief operational strategist, and primary catalyst driving the modern transformation and complete technical self-reliance of the Tanzania Railways Corporation (TRC) across key national and regional transit corridors.
A Cornerstone Alliance Catalyzing Regional Trade and Economic Independence
At the core of this milestone South Korea and Tanzania alliance lies Tanzania’s Central Corridor Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) project—a mega-scale transport initiative designed to link the Indian Ocean coast directly to the Great Lakes Region.
Following H.E. Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan’s landmark launching of the 506-kilometer Tabora-to-Kigoma SGR section in July 2026, the precision-engineered operational framework introduced through Korean technical leadership has sparked an unprecedented surge in domestic and cross-border trade efficiency.
Serving as the lead entity of an elite international consortium comprising eight global companies across five nations—including South Korea’s Cheil Engineering and Dong Myung Engineering, alongside other specialized engineering firms from overseas—KORAIL is directly orchestrating the deployment of high-capacity Electric Multiple Unit (EMU) locomotives and electric freight operations.
According to detailed estimates from Ministry of Transport officials, the state-of-the-art electric cargo trains introduced under Korean operational design can carry up to 10,000 tons of freight in a single trip—a monumental capacity equivalent to removing 500 heavy cargo trucks from the road network at once.
This massive logistics throughput is rapidly eliminating chronic bottlenecks at the Port of Dar es Salaam and other Indian Ocean maritime facilities in Tanzania.
By establishing faster cargo clearing pathways to the central and western zones, the South Korea-backed operational system is dramatically boosting transit traffic through Tanzanian lake ports to land linked neighboring states, including Burundi, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), and Zambia.
Crucially, this seamless rail connection addresses the growing trade demands of the DRC—the largest regional importer of Tanzanian food products and construction materials—thereby drastically slashing regional logistics costs, bolstering market competitiveness, and cementing Tanzania as the premier trade engine of East and Central Africa.
The commercial viability and operational performance achieved under this bilateral partnership have delivered immediate, historic milestones.
Within just the first six months of initial service, the SGR network safely transported 1.17 million passengers and generated over 30 billion Tanzanian Shillings in revenue.
By instilling a rigorous operational discipline that maintains an on-time performance rate exceeding 85 percent, Korea’s operational transfer enabled TRC to break a multi-year chronic deficit structure and achieve complete financial independence from government subsidies for the first time in 13 years.
Engineering Technological Sovereignty: South Korea as the Master Architect
South Korea’s engagement in Tanzania is defined by an unwavering commitment to technology transfer and genuine institutional independence.
As the sole public institution operating the vast national railway network in South Korea, KORAIL utilizes the exact same Electric Multiple Unit (EMU) train configurations deployed by TRC.
This direct technical alignment creates an ideal framework for South Korea to seamlessly transfer its world-renowned operational protocols and maintenance methodologies to Tanzania.
South Korea’s foundational involvement in the project began in 2017 with the successful execution of the Design and Construction Supervision Project for the Tanzania Central Line SGR.
Building upon this strong foundation, Korean rail authorities expanded their scope in 2022 by spearheading a comprehensive capacity-building and maintenance consulting initiative.
During this phase, Korean experts personally drafted and established TRC’s core internal regulations, general operating rules, and sophisticated maintenance manuals, effectively establishing the definitive national benchmark for Tanzanian railway operations.
“Our strategic partnership goes far beyond traditional engineering consulting; South Korea is actively building the technological foundation that will guarantee Tanzania’s total rail sovereignty,” declared Mr. Seong-il Kwon, KORAIL’s Country Director in Tanzania.
“By deploying 13 elite operational experts directly into the field and implementing tailored management regulations, we are empowering TRC’s workforce to independently manage, maintain, and expand their SGR network. I am entirely confident that Tanzania will emerge as the dominant, pivotal leader in the railway industry across all of Africa.”
Inter-Governmental Financing and Human Capital Development
Recognizing that sustainable infrastructure depends on human expertise, South Korea and Tanzania have structured an aggressive workforce development strategy for TRC.
Over a three-year period from 2022 to 2024, intensive, five-month railway maintenance and capacity-building training programs were executed in South Korea specifically tailored for TRC’s core engineering staff.
These immersive programs provided specialized education across critical domain areas, including railway administration, financial auditing, safety management systems, track maintenance technology, and advanced locomotive engineering.
To expand academic opportunities, Korean railway authorities established academic exchange partnerships that allow Tanzanian engineers and railway technicians to study at leading South Korean universities.
Looking ahead, South Korea is actively constructing a long-term educational ecosystem in Tanzania, which includes invitation-based training modules, specialized curriculum design, and the construction of a dedicated local training center for railway workers.
To secure the financial and physical infrastructure needed for long-term sustainability, the partnership leverages South Korean government financing mechanisms, including Economic Development Co-operation Fund (EDCF) loans and grant-based Official Development Assistance (ODA).
Key national initiatives spearheaded through this inter-governmental support include:
Pugu Station Comprehensive Maintenance Depot & Training Centre: Establishing a state-of-the-art facility at Pugu Station funded through EDCF loans to serve as the core hub for heavy railway equipment maintenance and the primary campus for cultivating TRC’s future technical talent.
Track Maintenance Technology Improvement Project: Implementing cutting-edge Korean track maintenance technology and advanced equipment under ODA grants to optimize line capacity, structural safety, and long-term track durability.
SGR Safety Management Capacity Building Project: Instituting rigorous safety standards and real-time monitoring systems to ensure hazard-free operations across all SGR passenger and cargo lines.
Unrivaled Global Excellence and Social Responsibility
South Korea’s transformational impact in Tanzania is backed by its unchallenged standing as a global railway leader.
Represented by KORAIL—a 100 percent state-owned public institution and the Chair Organization for the Asia-Pacific region within the International Union of Railways (UIC)—Korea sets international standards in railway diplomacy and operational efficiency.
In South Korea, a massive, high-density national network spanning 69 high-speed stations (596.3 kilometers), 267 conventional stations (3,551.4 km), and 275 metropolitan subway stations (741.4 km) is managed with absolute precision.
On a daily basis, Korea safely controls 3,340 train operations—including 369 high-speed KTX trains, 299 conventional trains, 2,591 subway trains, and 171 freight trains.
Remarkably, this network achieves an unprecedented 99.46 percent UIC punctuality rate and maintains an astonishingly low accident rate of just 0.0136 per million train-kilometers, powered by advanced Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) Condition-Based Maintenance (CBM) technologies.
Applying this world-class technological expertise globally, South Korea is actively executing major railway development projects across 10 countries worldwide:
Africa:
Joint electric train management and maintenance consulting with the Moroccan National Railway (ONCF), alongside railway signaling modernization along Egypt’s Cairo-to-Beni Suef line.
Asia & Pacific:
Complete operations and maintenance (O&M) for Manila Metro Rail Transit Line 7 (MRT-7) in the Philippines; High-Speed Rolling Stock O&M contracts and the Tashkent-Samarkand High-Speed Railway feasibility study in Uzbekistan and Locomotive Maintenance Technology Transfer and ODA projects in Bangladesh.
There is also foundational infrastructure maintenance, Traffic Control Centre (RTCC) master planning, and Metro Project Management Consulting (PMC) services in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia; urban railway legal framework development and training center advisory in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam; and Mandalay-to-Myitkyina rail improvement supervision alongside passenger car procurement consulting in Myanmar.
Corporate Social Responsibility
Beyond technical excellence, South Korea actively fulfills its Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) as a “Partner for Mutual Growth” in Tanzania. Demonstrating its deep commitment to local communities, KORAIL’s Tanzania branch recently established a fully equipped electronic library at Leena Prim

articles.title: Debt crisis drives 8% cut in education spending in high-debt countries - Debt Justice
articles.summary: Debt crisis drives 8% cut in education spending in high-debt countries  Debt Justice
articles.full_text:
Education spending has fallen by 8% in countries facing the highest risk of debt distress since 2019, according to new research by Debt Justice, as lower-income countries in debt crisis face brutal cuts in spending on healthcare and education.
The cuts mean that governments are spending 50% less than the level needed to meet the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030.[1]
The figures are being released ahead of the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok from 12 to 18 October, where the UK government is expected to announce plans for its G20 presidency in 2027.
Heidi Chow, Executive Director of Debt Justice, said:
“High levels of debt are having a devastating impact on people’s access to healthcare and education. We urgently need debt cancellation – especially from the highest interest lenders like banks, hedge funds and oil traders. The UK government must use its presidency of the G20 next year to seek agreement on a fast, effective and fair debt cancellation scheme.”
Catherine Mithia from the African Forum and Network on Debt and Development (Afrodad), said:
“This research confirms the human cost of debt. Governments in high-debt countries are being forced to cut education and health spending, because the world lacks adequate mechanisms for timely, coordinated and equitable debt restructuring for low- and middle-income countries.  During its G20 presidency in 2027, the UK has a chance to lead reforms of the G20 Common Framework to allow debt suspension during negotiations and to pass legislation in the UK that limits private creditors seeking recoveries through UK courts during restructuring.”
Souleymane Gueye, from the Senegalese campaign group FRAPP, said:
“In Senegal, half of our revenue goes to creditors. Education and healthcare share barely a quarter. This is no longer a budget; it is a ransom.”
The research finds that in lower-income countries the IMF classifies as in debt distress or at high risk of being so, education spending has been cut by on average 8%, and health spending by 1%, since 2019. Overall public spending has been cut by 2%. Spending in lower-debt burden countries has increased, but at a far slower rate than is likely to be needed to meet the Sustainable Development Goals.
Graph. Growth needed in public spending needed to meet the Sustainable Development Goals, contrasted with actual growth in spending by debt risk category
External debt burdens have increased in recent years due to the Covid crisis, the global rise in interest rates, climate disasters and now the rise in energy and essential import costs due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the IMF, has said the current rise in global interest rates is worsening the debt problem in lower income countries.[2]
In 2020 the G20 created a debt relief scheme, the Common Framework for Debt Treatments. In September 2026 Senegal became just the fifth country to apply for debt relief through the scheme.
The other four countries have all suffered from slow and inadequate relief, with private creditors a major obstacle. Chad received no debt relief after its main private creditor, Glencore, refused to negotiate. Ethiopia was pressured into paying more when vulture funds began the process of suing the East African country in the UK High Court.[3]
African governments have said the G20 Framework “has not provided a pathway towards the quick restoration of debt sustainability, creating some considerable scepticism as to its potential to deliver effectively for highly indebted countries, particularly in Africa”.[4]
In Kenya, real government spending per person on education has been cut by 9% since 2019, and health spending by 26%. Kenya is rated as at high risk of debt distress by the IMF. External debt payments are over 20% of government revenue. Of Kenya’s external debt payments, 47% are to private lenders, 30% to other governments and 23% to multilateral institutions.[5]
Senegal faces a similar problem. Of Senegal’s external debt payments in 2026, 62% are to private lenders, 25% to multilateral institutions and 12% to other governments.[6]
Notes
[1] Debt Justice’s briefing ‘How external debt burdens are helping drive cuts in spending on healthcare and education’ is available at https://debtjustice.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Health-and-education-spending_10.26.pdf
All the calculations in this research are publicly available at https://debtjustice.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Public-spending_09.26.xlsx
[3] Save the Children and Debt Justice’s report ‘Now is The Time to Act: Six Reforms for the G20 Common Framework for Debt Treatments’ is available at https://resourcecentre.savethechildren.net/document/now-is-the-time-to-act-six-reforms-for-the-g20-common-framework-for-debt-treatments
[4] The Common African Position on Debt was agreed by the African Union in February 2026 https://au.int/sites/default/files/decisions/46189-EX_CL_Decisions_E.pdf
It is available at: https://afrodad.org/afcodd6/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Common-African-Position-CAP-On-Debt.pdf
[6] Calculated from World Bank International Debt Statistics database.

articles.title: ‘Africa Must Stop Exporting Raw Materials’ –Ex-AfDB President Adesina Calls For Industrialisation, Technology Innovation - Sahara Reporters
articles.summary: ‘Africa Must Stop Exporting Raw Materials’ –Ex-AfDB President Adesina Calls For Industrialisation, Technology Innovation  Sahara Reporters
articles.full_text:
According to him, the continent’s long-term prosperity depends on its ability to build productive economies, create value from its resources and strengthen its industrial capacity.
Former President of the African Development Bank (AfDB), Akinwumi Adesina, has called on African countries to move beyond exporting raw materials and prioritise industrialisation, local manufacturing and technological innovation to accelerate the continent’s economic development.
Adesina made the call while delivering an address at the BPI Iconic Awards in Johannesburg, South Africa, on October 8, 2026.
He argued that Africa must rethink its economic model by processing its natural resources locally, developing industries and investing in technology rather than continuing to export raw materials for processing elsewhere.
According to him, the continent’s long-term prosperity depends on its ability to build productive economies, create value from its resources and strengthen its industrial capacity.
Adesina also highlighted the importance of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), saying stronger economic integration could help African countries expand markets, improve trade and support industrial development.
He stressed that technology and artificial intelligence would be important to Africa’s economic transformation, urging leaders to embrace innovation and prepare their countries for an increasingly technology-driven global economy.
The former AfDB president also emphasised the importance of investing in people, declaring that “Africa’s greatest asset is its people.”
He said Africa’s young population represented a major opportunity for development, provided governments and businesses invested in the skills, education and opportunities needed to harness their potential.
Adesina further underscored the need for visionary and ethical leadership, arguing that the interests of citizens and countries should take precedence over narrower interests.
“The national interest must stand above all other interests,” he said.
He also pointed to large-scale industrial investments as examples of the kind of projects that could help change Africa’s economic trajectory.
Among the examples he cited was the Dangote Refinery, a $20 billion industrial project in Nigeria, which he presented as an illustration of the scale of investment needed to expand local processing and manufacturing capacity.
Adesina’s remarks come amid continuing calls for African countries to reduce their dependence on exporting unprocessed commodities and instead develop industries that generate jobs, strengthen domestic economies and retain more value within the continent.
For many African economies, the export of raw materials remains a major source of foreign exchange. However, limited local processing and manufacturing capacity mean that much of the value created from those resources is generated outside the continent.
Expanding industrial production, Adesina’s message suggested, would require more than access to natural resources. It would also depend on investment, technological development, effective leadership and policies that support businesses and regional trade.
His emphasis on the AfCFTA also points to the potential role of a more integrated African market in supporting local industries, enabling businesses to reach more consumers and making it easier for countries to trade with one another.
The agreement is intended to create a single continental market for goods and services, although its potential benefits depend on effective implementation and the removal of barriers to trade between African countries.
Adesina’s address placed industrialisation, technology and human capital at the centre of the debate over Africa’s economic future, urging leaders to focus on building economies capable of producing goods, creating value and competing in global markets.

articles.title: Anwar: Malaysia, Egypt to expand trade, investment and economic cooperation - The Edge Malaysia
articles.summary: Anwar: Malaysia, Egypt to expand trade, investment and economic cooperation  The Edge Malaysia
articles.full_text:
PUTRAJAYA (Oct 10): Malaysia and Egypt will focus on expanding trade and investment cooperation, improving flight connectivity and exploring new areas of economic collaboration at a Joint Commission meeting in the first quarter of next year.
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said the meeting, agreed upon by the two countries’ foreign ministers, would provide a platform to translate growing bilateral ties into broader economic opportunities.
He said bilateral trade had increased 74.7% this year, but stressed that the growth came from a low base, leaving considerable room for further expansion.
“We have achieved this phenomenal increase this year, rising to 74.7% of trade, but then it is from a very, very low base,” said the prime minister.
Anwar was speaking at a joint press conference with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi in conjunction with El-Sisi’s two-day state visit to Malaysia.
He said Malaysia saw considerable potential to expand cooperation with Egypt in several sectors, including semiconductors, electrical and electronics (E&E), agriculture and pharmaceuticals.
Malaysia was also looking at emerging economies, including BRICS countries, as potential sources of pharmaceutical products, with Egypt among the countries that could meet its needs.
“Egypt has the potential to become a destination for sourcing pharmaceuticals,” said Anwar.
He said improved air connectivity, including more regular flights, would also be important in facilitating trade, investment and tourism between the two countries.
Anwar described Egypt as an important country in the Arab world and Africa, adding that closer engagement would give Malaysia greater opportunities to expand its economic presence in the region.
Earlier, the prime minister and his counterpart held a four-eyed meeting at the Seri Perdana Complex here on Saturday, marking a significant step towards elevating Malaysia-Egypt relations to a strategic partnership after more than six decades of diplomatic ties.
The meeting, held in conjunction with El-Sisi’s two-day state visit to Malaysia, provided an opportunity for both leaders to review bilateral cooperation, explore new areas of collaboration and exchange views on regional and international developments of mutual interest.
The Egyptian president, who is undertaking his first state visit to Malaysia since assuming office in June 2014, arrived at the complex at 12.58pm for a series of official engagements aimed at strengthening political, economic and diplomatic relations between the two nations.
In 2025, Egypt was Malaysia’s seventh-largest trading partner in Africa, with total bilateral trade valued at RM3.08 billion (US$0.72 billion).
Malaysia’s exports to Egypt amounted to RM2.55 billion (US$0.60 billion), while imports totalled RM530 million (US$0.12 billion).
From January to August 2026, bilateral trade surged 74.7% to RM3.49 billion (US$0.87 billion).

articles.title: Ghana and Russia Explore a Science and Technology Partnership ‎ - Modern Ghana
articles.summary: Ghana and Russia Explore a Science and Technology Partnership ‎  Modern Ghana
articles.full_text:
On 8 October 2026, H.E. Andrei Ordash, Ambassador of the Russian Federation to Ghana, paid a courtesy call on Dr. Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, Minister of Environment, Science and Technology. The two sides discussed cooperation in advancing science, adopting advanced technologies, and building partnerships between universities and research centres in both countries.
A relationship with deep roots
The visit builds on cordial diplomatic relations that have existed since 1958. At Russia Day celebrations in Accra in June, both countries reaffirmed their commitment to deeper cooperation in trade, investment, energy, agriculture, education and technology.
Ghana's Foreign Ministry has also expressed its commitment to strengthening these ties, particularly in education, energy and multilateral cooperation, while encouraging more collaboration in trade, investment and technology.
Education as a bridge
Ambassador Ordash has described human capital development as central to Russia's engagement with Ghana, with plans to expand scholarships, youth exchanges, academic partnerships and professional training. He has said that more than 600 Ghanaian students are currently studying in Russia. A scientific partnership between universities would naturally extend this tradition of academic exchange.
An economic and technological context
The ambassador has said Russia hopes to move beyond traditional trade through long-term investment, joint ventures and technology partnerships. Reports put bilateral trade at about US$800 million. He has also said that trade and investment remain below their potential. Ghana, for its part, is interested in access to technology to modernise its economy, not only in commodity trade. Science and technology cooperation fits that shared interest.
A timely moment
The meeting comes ahead of the third Russia-Africa Summit, scheduled for late October 2026. Ghana has said it looks forward to increased engagement through the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum and the summit.
Looking ahead
At this stage, the discussions express shared goodwill and interest. The ministry may wish to share more detail as talks progress, such as which institutions might take part, what forms of cooperation are envisaged, and how any partnership will serve Ghana's national development priorities. Such clarity would help students, researchers and the wider public follow the process and take full advantage of it.
Ghana has long pursued friendship with all nations. If it is guided by mutual respect, transparency and the interests of Ghanaian institutions, a scientific partnership with Russia could be a constructive addition to the country's international collaborations.

articles.title: Where capital moves next: RISE Summit 2026 brings global investment leaders to Dubai - Zawya
articles.summary: Where capital moves next: RISE Summit 2026 brings global investment leaders to Dubai  Zawya
articles.full_text:
- José Manuel Barroso and Ludovic Subran lead Global Leaders Series discussions on the changing global investment map
Dubai, UAE: Government leaders, global institutional investors, sovereign funds and major developers will converge in Dubai this week to explore where capital is moving and where the biggest opportunities lie as geopolitical uncertainty and changing trade flows recalibrate investment priorities across markets, infrastructure, cities, real estate and the experience economy.
The inaugural RISE Summit 2026 on 14 October at Dubai World Trade Centre will gather more than 250 senior delegates to explore how capital can recharge momentum in global economies, connecting investment strategy with the sectors shaping the next phase of economic and urban growth.
The one-day summit arrives as Dubai’s economy rebounds following months of regional disruption. The emirate’s non-oil private sector Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) rose to 54.5 in September, its strongest reading of 2026, according to S&P Global, while real estate sales of AED 379 billion in the first nine months of the year were the second-highest on record for the period, based on Dubai Land Department data.
Business and capital continue to flow into the emirate and the wider region, with the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) surpassing 10,000 active registered companies for the first time in the first half of 2026, while Gulf sovereign wealth funds deployed a record US$53.9 billion over the same period, according to Global SWF.
Global Leaders Series: where capital moves next
The Global Leaders Series (GLS) will bring two headline international conversations to RISE Summit 2026, examining how economic realignment and changing financial conditions are reshaping the deployment of long-term capital.
José Manuel Barroso, Chairman of International Advisors at Goldman Sachs and former President of the European Commission, will lead ‘The Great Capital Shift’, exploring how the United States, Europe, Asia and the Gulf are competing for long-term capital and whether current shifts represent a temporary adjustment or a lasting redrawing of the global investment map.
Ludovic Subran, Group Chief Investment Officer & Chief Economist, Allianz, will tackle ‘Long-Term Capital in a Higher-Rate World’, examining how changing rates, inflation and risk are influencing allocations across fixed income, real estate, infrastructure and private markets.
UAE leadership and Dubai’s growth story
The UAE and Dubai leadership will bring a regional perspective on investment, economic diversification and Dubai’s continued development as a global centre for business and capital.
H.E. Abdulla bin Touq Al Marri, Minister of Economy & Tourism, UAE, will examine how economic resilience can translate into new investment partnerships and sustainable growth in ‘From Resilience to Opportunity in a Realigning World’ after H.E. Omar Bu Shehab, Director General, Dubai Land Department, delivers the official opening address at RISE Summit 2026.
H.E. Helal Saeed Almarri, Director General of the Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism, will explore the foundations of Dubai’s economic model and the D33 agenda through ‘Built to Compound: Dubai’s Economic Model and the D33 Agenda.’
Dubai’s development story will also feature Mohamed Alabbar, Founder & Managing Director, Emaar Properties, who will bring the perspective of one of the region’s leading developers in ‘Building Through the Cycle’, examining long-term investment and development through changing market conditions, and Khalid Al Malik, Chief Executive Officer, Dubai Holding Real Estate, examining the master plans shaping Dubai’s next phase of urban growth.
Dubai’s next phase of growth will also be examined through sessions focused on mobility and market regulation. Muna Al Osaimi, Chief Executive Officer, Strategy & Corporate Governance Sector, Roads and Transport Authority (RTA), will lead ‘Land, Mobility and the Making of Dubai’s Next Growth Corridors’, examining how transport and infrastructure are opening new areas of growth across the city. H.E. Abdulla Ahmed Mohammed Saleh Al Shehhi, Chief Executive Officer, Real Estate Regulatory Agency (RERA), will address market regulation, transparency and investor protection in ‘Trust as an Asset: Regulating a Market the World Is Watching’.
Capital, cities and real assets
Across the wider programme, RISE Summit 2026 will examine how capital is moving into infrastructure, real estate, hospitality, tourism and new forms of urban investment.

By: Business Today Staff
Sun, Oct. 11, 2026
S&P Global Ratings has affirmed Egypt’s long- and short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings at B/B, maintaining a stable outlook, supported by exchange rate flexibility, improving foreign currency inflows, ongoing fiscal consolidation, and continued economic reforms.
In its latest report, the agency said the stable outlook reflects a balance between Egypt’s medium-term economic growth prospects and continued reform efforts on one hand, and risks stemming from prolonged regional conflict and elevated energy prices on the other.
However, the agency warned that a prolonged conflict and persistently high energy prices could intensify inflationary pressures, delay further interest rate cuts, and increase debt-servicing costs, potentially limiting the government’s ability to strengthen its fiscal position.
Egypt has also exceeded the fiscal targets outlined under its International Monetary Fund (IMF) program, achieving a primary budget surplus equivalent to 4.9% of GDP in fiscal year 2025/2026.
The government has reaffirmed its commitment to IMF-backed reforms, including maintaining exchange rate flexibility, increasing domestic revenue mobilization, accelerating divestments from state-owned assets, and strengthening private-sector participation.
S&P highlighted the resilience of Egypt’s external position despite higher energy import costs, supported by strong exports, rising remittances from Egyptians abroad, sustained tourism revenues, and a recovery in Suez Canal receipts.
Suez Canal revenues reached $3.4 billion during the first nine months of FY2025/2026, compared with $2.8 billion in the corresponding period a year earlier, although receipts remained below levels recorded before the Red Sea disruptions that began in 2023.
Foreign investors’ holdings of Egyptian pound-denominated government debt securities increased to $34.5 billion in September 2026, up from $22.2 billion in April, but remained below their February peak of $39.1 billion.
The recovery in foreign portfolio inflows enabled the Central Bank of Egypt (CBE) to purchase foreign currency from the market, helping international reserve assets reach a record $54.5 billion in September, according to S&P's figures.
Meanwhile, the banking sector’s net foreign assets rose to $31.2 billion, their highest level in six years.
S&P considers banks’ positive net foreign asset position an important buffer against external shocks, potentially allowing the financial system to absorb additional capital outflows before they directly affect the central bank’s international reserves.
S&P expects disruptions across the Middle East to persist into 2027, with regional oil and gas flows remaining below pre-conflict levels through the end of next year.
Egypt is also working to diversify its crude oil import sources. Saudi Arabia accounted for 66% of Egypt’s oil imports in FY2025/2026, down from 89% in the previous fiscal year.
The agency noted that hedging contracts partially mitigate the impact of oil price volatility on Egypt’s import bill.
S&P estimates that Egypt’s current account deficit will reach approximately 5% of GDP in FY2026/2027, compared with 5.1% in the previous fiscal year and 4.2% in FY2024/2025.
The projected deficit reflects the persistence of the trade imbalance and higher energy import costs, despite strong tourism revenues, remittance inflows, and recovering Suez Canal receipts.
Egypt’s annual headline inflation accelerated to 15.2% in March 2026 before easing to 14.5% in August, compared with a 43-month low of 11.7% recorded in September 2025.
The Central Bank of Egypt reduced interest rates by a cumulative 825 basis points between April 2025 and February 2026, before pausing its monetary easing cycle as rising food and energy prices renewed inflationary pressures.
In September 2026, the central bank maintained its overnight deposit and lending rates at 19% and 20%, respectively.
S&P expects inflation to average 12.9% in FY2026/2027, although elevated energy prices remain a significant upside risk. The agency also anticipates a slower decline in yields on domestic government debt instruments.
Interest payments are projected to account for approximately 60% of government revenues in FY2026/2027 and 53% in the following fiscal year, down from 68% in FY2025/2026.
The agency expects inflation to average around 12% over FY2026/2027 and FY2027/2028 before declining to approximately 9% by FY2028/2029.
Egypt’s economy expanded by an estimated 5.1% in real terms during FY2025/2026, marking its strongest growth rate in three years, according to S&P.
However, the agency expects economic growth to moderate to 4.5% in FY2026/2027.
S&P attributed the previous fiscal year's strong performance to growth in non-oil manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade, information and communications technology, and tourism.
Household consumption also benefited from higher remittances from Egyptians working abroad, relatively lower inflation, and stable labor market conditions.
Looking ahead, the agency expects continued economic reforms and exchange rate flexibility to support Egypt’s competitiveness over the medium term.
S&P emphasized that sustaining strong economic growth will require faster structural reforms and greater private-sector participation.
Key priorities include reducing the size of the informal economy, improving governance, transparency, and financial disclosure among state-owned enterprises, and removing barriers to competition.
The government is preparing several companies for partial divestment through sales to investors.
Meanwhile, the CBE has discontinued subsidized lending programs for state-owned enterprises to improve credit allocation.
Authorities have also tightened oversight of the costs and financing arrangements of import-intensive public investment projects.
The government expects to generate an additional $1.5 billion from its state asset divestment program by December 2026.
Planned transactions include the sale of the state’s entire stake in the Gabal El-Zeit wind farm for $420 million, alongside partial sales of the Finance Ministry’s holdings in listed state-owned companies valued at $106 million.
Expected divestments involving Banque du Caire and Misr Life Insurance are also anticipated to generate additional resources that could be directed toward reducing public debt.
These targets follow approximately $2.2 billion in divestment proceeds generated during 2022 and 2023, as well as a $3.5 billion Qatari real estate investment transaction concluded in late 2025.
S&P noted that Egypt expanded its IMF financing arrangement to $8 billion in March 2024, with the program subsequently extended through December 2026.
The IMF completed the program’s seventh review in July 2026, allowing Egypt to receive a $1.7 billion financing tranche.
The eighth and final tranche, also worth $1.7 billion, is expected to be disbursed in December 2026.
The agency does not expect Egypt to pursue a new IMF financing arrangement after the current program expires, although it anticipates continued close cooperation through a domestically driven economic reform agenda.
Egypt also benefits from international financing and investment packages, including the European Union’s €7.4 billion support package covering 2024–2028.
The package comprises €5 billion in macro-financial assistance and budget-support loans, €1.8 billion in private-sector investment guarantees, and €600 million in development grants.
S&P also expects continued concessional financing from the World Bank, African Development Bank, and Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.
S&P expects Gulf Cooperation Council countries to maintain financial support for Egypt, citing Cairo’s strategic importance in the region and its role in facilitating humanitarian assistance to Gaza.
The agency noted that Gulf support has increasingly shifted from deposits and unconditional financial assistance toward foreign direct investment linked to specific projects and assets.
Major investments include Abu Dhabi-based ADQ’s $35 billion commitment to the Ras El Hekma development project in early 2024.
Egypt also reached an agreement with Qatar in November 2025 involving a $30 billion investment to develop the Alam El Roum area on the North Coast over seven years.
These investments are expected to support foreign currency liquidity while contributing to economic development and private-sector activity.
S&P said fiscal consolidation measures helped reduce Egypt’s overall budget deficit to 5.8% of GDP in FY2025/2026, alongside a primary surplus of 4.9%.
Measures to broaden the tax base, improve compliance, and simplify tax dispute settlements increased government revenues by an amount equivalent to 0.9% of GDP during the fiscal year.
Increases in fuel, natural gas, and electricity prices also helped contain the energy subsidy bill at approximately EGP 196 billion, equivalent to 0.9% of GDP.
These measures were accompanied by a limited expansion of cash and in-kind assistance for vulnerable households under the Takaful and Karama social protection program.
The agency noted that this approach aims to balance spending restraint with more efficient subsidy allocation and measures to cushion vulnerable groups against rising living costs.

articles.title: India and Europe: Bridging Continents Through IMEC - CSEP India
articles.summary: India and Europe: Bridging Continents Through IMEC  CSEP India
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary
Reconnecting India and Europe in an Era of Fragmentation
In a world adrift, marked by conflict and fragmentation, India and Europe represent a rare example of intensifying cooperation and geoeconomic convergence. As two of the largest economies and democracies in the world, the European Union (EU) and India will need to craft new, interoperable systems and instruments for economic interdependence to advance their convergence.
As this volume shows, the successful implementation of the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) as an Indo-Atlantic connectivity partnership between India and Europe will require far more than investments in ports, railways, and logistics infrastructure. It will depend equally on policy coordination, regulatory interoperability, digital integration, institutional governance, financial structuring, and sustained political engagement across all participating geographies and beyond, including adjacent regions: from Southeast Asia to the North Atlantic and from Central Asia to North and East Africa.
IMEC emerged amid intensifying geopolitical fragmentation and growing concern about the resilience of global trade, energy, and digital networks. Since its announcement in 2023, the war in Ukraine, conflict in Gaza, disruptions in the Red Sea, and the Strait of Hormuz crisis have exposed the risks created by concentrated trade routes and strategic chokepoints. In parallel, India and Europe have deepened economic and strategic cooperation through the conclusion of negotiations on the India–EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) and a broader agenda focused on supply-chain resilience, connectivity, and economic security.
In this context, IMEC has evolved from a connectivity initiative into a wider resilience project. While originally conceived as a multimodal corridor linking India, the Gulf, and Europe through transport, energy, and digital infrastructure, its strategic significance today extends beyond logistics. The corridor has become a test case for whether India, Europe, and their regional partners can build new frameworks for economic interdependence capable of operating in an increasingly unstable international environment.
The central conclusion of this volume is that India and the European Union should not pursue IMEC as a mere transport corridor but as a resilient economic network connecting India, Europe, and West Asia through interoperable infrastructure, energy systems, digital platforms, investment mechanisms, regulatory cooperation, and shared security arrangements.
From Corridor to Economic Network
IMEC should not be treated as a single route, a geopolitical symbol, or a substitute for the Suez Canal. It should be developed as a flexible and adaptive network that provides redundancy, optionality, and resilience.
Developed independently across different geographies and sectors, the contributions reflect European, planning, logistics, and strategic perspectives, yet converge on a conclusion: IMEC should provide route diversification, multimodal redundancy, interoperable systems, and wider regional integration. Together, these elements support a broader conception of IMEC as an economic network rather than a transport line. The same holds true for India’s interests in IMEC This network logic applies across multiple domains. Physical infrastructure requires alternative port access points, complementary maritime gateways, and redundancy in routing. Digital systems require interoperable customs platforms, payments architecture, and data standards. Energy connectivity requires interconnected electricity grids, green-hydrogen corridors, and cross-border regulatory cooperation. Security depends on coordinated approaches to maritime protection, critical infrastructure resilience, and crisis response.
These principles provide the basis for assessing IMEC’s economic, security, energy, climate, and political dividends. New Delhi, Brussels and European capitals will have to coordinate policy across these different domains.
The Four Strategic Dividends of IMEC
This report shows that IMEC could serve as a catalyst to reconnect Europe and India after decades of divergence and disruption. From a geoeconomic perspective, IMEC should form the strategic heart of a broader India-EU connectivity partnership towards linking the Indian and Atlantic oceans. The success of this Indo-Atlantic economic initiative rests on four dividends.
Economic Dividend
The economic case for IMEC rests on reducing transit time, uncertainty, and trade frictions. Modelling presented in this volume suggests that a 40% reduction in transit time between India and Europe could add approximately US$3.535 billion to India’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP). The gains would extend across manufacturing, electronics, textiles, automotive components, and selected agricultural exports.
Beyond direct trade gains, IMEC could strengthen regional value chains, improve competitiveness, support implementation of the India–EU FTA, and accelerate integration with Gulf and European markets.
Security Dividend
The corridor’s strategic relevance has increased because of repeated disruptions affecting maritime trade routes. IMEC offers an opportunity to diversify logistics pathways, reduce exposure to chokepoints, strengthen maritime cooperation, and develop coordinated approaches to infrastructure protection. EU–India cooperation in the Gulf and Western Indian Ocean demonstrates the growing importance of this security dimension.
Energy and Climate Dividend
The corridor could support renewable-energy trade, electricity interconnections, green-hydrogen exports, and wider climate cooperation between Europe, the Gulf, and South Asia. Several contributions emphasise that energy connectivity should be treated as a core pillar of IMEC rather than an ancillary component. Climate resilience, water cooperation, and cross-border energy systems increasingly form part of the corridor’s long-term value proposition.
Political and Stabilisation Dividend
IMEC’s political significance extends beyond its economic effects. The Peace Triangle framework suggests that shared infrastructure, economic interdependence, climate cooperation, and security coordination could create incentives for cooperation among Israel, Palestine, and Jordan. This contribution would be enabling rather than determinative: infrastructure cannot resolve political conflicts, but it can help create conditions in which agreements are more sustainable. As the first global connectivity partnership between India and the EU, IMEC also offers a platform for New Delhi and Brussels to coordinate and align their economic and security policies for the Middle East and adjacent regions.
The Missing Layer: Governance
One of the clearest findings of the compendium is that IMEC’s primary challenge is no longer conceptual but institutional. Political support is significant, infrastructure plans are advancing in several jurisdictions, and digital pilots have begun; however, implementation remains fragmented because the corridor lacks a common framework for coordinating governments, financiers, regulators, technical experts, and private-sector actors.
The immediate requirement is a common execution framework that addresses governance, project preparation, financing coordination, regulatory interoperability, and implementation. Such a framework must connect governments, financiers, regulators, technical experts, and private-sector actors around agreed priorities and delivery mechanisms.
Proposed solutions converge around three institutional innovations:
- National Sherpas or envoys to coordinate implementation;
- Stronger domestic planning mechanisms, including Gati-Shakti Transport and Logistics Planning and Research Authority (GTLPRA)-type frameworks;
- Track 1.5 structures to bridge expert research and formal decision-making.
The broader lesson is that physical connectivity will deliver corridor-wide benefits only if participating countries also make their governance, regulatory, and implementation systems interoperable.
The Digital and Regulatory Challenge
IMEC’s digital foundations are as important as its physical infrastructure because trade, logistics, customs, payments, and investment increasingly depend on the secure movement of information.
Regulatory fragmentation could prevent the corridor’s physical assets from functioning as an integrated system. Divergences between India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA) and Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) create uncertainty around logistics data sharing, while different approaches to digital identity, payments, data governance, and privacy complicate interoperability. Fragmented customs systems, differing digital-trade provisions, and uncertainty over subsea-cable governance add further constraints.
Yet the volume also identifies pathways forward. Expansion of Master Application for International Trade and Regulatory Interface (MAITRI) as a corridor-wide customs interface, greater use of interoperable payment platforms, Project Nexus integration, trusted data-transfer arrangements, and deeper cooperation through the EU–India Trade and Technology Council all provide opportunities for building a shared digital layer.
A Six-Point Action Agenda
This volume identifies six mutually reinforcing priorities for Indian, European, and regional policymakers. Together, they provide an implementation agenda spanning corridor design, institutional coordination, digital interoperability, investment, energy and climate cooperation, and security.
- Develop IMEC as a network rather than a fixed route. Build redundancy through multiple ports, complementary corridors, and flexible routing options.
- Establish formal architecture for implementation. Create Sherpa mechanisms, structured ministerial coordination, and Track 1.5 execution frameworks that can convert political commitments into actionable programmes.
- Accelerate interoperability

Prime Minister Narendra Modi will inaugurate several infrastructure projects and lay foundation stones for new initiatives across Tamil Nadu on Sunday. As per a release, at around 11:30 AM, he will undertake a ride on the Chennai Metro from Porur Bypass Station to Poonamallee Bypass Station and back. At around 12:15 PM, he will perform Darshan and Pooja at the Jalakandeswarar Temple in Chennai. Thereafter, he will undertake a walkthrough of the Brain Centre at IIT Madras.
At around 1:30 PM, the Prime Minister will lay the foundation stone of, inaugurate and dedicate various development projects worth over Rs 13,000 crore. He will also address the gathering on the occasion. At around 3 PM, he will participate in the Golden Jubilee celebrations of Jaigopal Garodia Hindu Vidyalaya Matriculation Higher Secondary School in Chennai and address the gathering. Prime Minister will inaugurate the Poonamallee-Vadapalani stretch of Phase II of the Chennai Metro Rail Project, built at a cost of around Rs 4,900 crore. The corridor features a unique 3.7-km double-decker structure. It also features advanced signalling systems designed to support driverless operations. It is expected to reduce daily travel time for commuters and improve connectivity between Chennai’s rapidly growing western suburbs and the city centre, the release said.
Prime Minister will lay the foundation stone of and inaugurate key National Highway projects worth around Rs 3,700 crore. These projects will strengthen road connectivity, reduce travel time, ease traffic congestion and support economic growth in the State. Prime Minister will inaugurate the 36-km, four-laned Vadugapatti-Therkuvenganallur section of NH-744. The project will improve connectivity to important pilgrimage, industrial and commercial centres in the region, facilitating smoother movement of people and goods. He will also inaugurate the 30-km, four-laned Madurai Ring Road section of NH-744A. The project will improve traffic movement around Madurai and help ease congestion within the city, the release said.
Prime Minister will lay the foundation stone of the four-lane Thiruvarur Bypass on the Nagapattinam-Thanjavur section of NH-83. The project will strengthen road connectivity in Thiruvarur and facilitate smoother traffic movement by providing an alternative route around the town. Prime Minister will dedicate and inaugurate railway infrastructure projects worth over Rs 750 crore. He will dedicate the Karaikal-Peralam railway line, further strengthening rail connectivity in the region. He will also dedicate three rail flyovers in Coimbatore and surrounding areas.
These will ease congestion at busy level crossings, reduce waiting time and improve road safety for commuters. Prime Minister will also inaugurate five Amrit Stations at Palani, Vellore Cantonment, Ambasamudram, Paramakkudi and Namakkal, which have been redeveloped under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme, the release said. Prime Minister will inaugurate and lay the foundation stone of several port-related projects in Tamil Nadu to strengthen maritime infrastructure, expand cargo-handling capacity and improve logistics efficiency.
He will inaugurate four infrastructure projects at Chennai Port: a Paved Storage Yard, four EXIM Godowns, an upgraded Cruise Terminal and a Seafarers Club. These projects will improve cargo storage and handling, expand warehouse capacity, modernise passenger facilities to enable the simultaneous embarkation and disembarkation of more cruise passengers, and provide modern welfare, recreational and support facilities for visiting seafarers and maritime personnel. Prime Minister will inaugurate and lay the foundation stones for eight major development projects at V.O. Chidambaranar Port. The projects will expand cargo and container capacity, build infrastructure for the transition to cleaner maritime energy, and improve the efficiency of cargo evacuation and logistics within the Port ecosystem. Prime Minister will also inaugurate the Coal Berth-3 project and lay the foundation stone for capital dredging works for Container Terminal Phase-I, Stage-II at Kamarajar Port, the release said.
Prime Minister will lay the foundation stone of the Group II/III Lube Oil Base Stocks (LOBS) project at the existing Manali Refinery of Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) in Chennai. With a total cost of around Rs 1,620 crore and a capacity of 270 thousand metric tonnes per annum (TMTPA), the project aims to produce Group II/III Lube Oil Base Stocks for the manufacture of world-class, premium-quality lubricants in India. Prime Minister will dedicate to the nation the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre (SGBC) at IIT Madras. He will also launch its pioneering global scientific mission to map more than 100 human brains into three-dimensional atlases at cellular resolution, across the human lifespan - from the foetal stage to old age. Prime Minister will also release C-STROKE, a one-of-a-kind human ischaemic stroke atlas. Featuring over 1,000 annotated microscopic sections from a stroke-affected brain, the atlas will help researchers worldwide identify novel therapeutic targets.
Prime Minister will participate in the Golden Jubilee celebrations of Jaigopal Garodia Hindu Vidyalaya Matriculation Higher Secondary School in Chennai. The Golden Jubilee marks five decades of the institution’s contribution to education and its role in nurturing generations of students through academic excellence, discipline, cultural values and holistic education, the release said. Guided by its motto, “Sa Vidya Ya Vimuktaye” (Knowledge that liberates), the school seeks to nurture individuals who make meaningful contributions to society. (ANI)

articles.full_text:
The federal government plans to increase Nigeria's vehicle demand met by local assemblers from less than 8 per cent to 70 per cent, aiming to boost domestic manufacturing, create jobs, and reduce reliance on imported vehicles and parts. The National Automotive Design and Development Council (NADDC) outlined a phased approach to this goal, with the Bureau of Public Procurement directing all federal entities to prioritize Nigerian-assembled vehicles. This initiative supports both economic growth and compliance with African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) rules.
The federal government plans to raise the share of Nigeria's vehicle demand met by local assemblers from less than 8 per cent to 70 per cent, in a push to boost domestic manufacturing, create jobs and cut reliance on imported vehicles and parts.
The director-general of the National Automotive Design and Development Council (NADDC), Joseph Osanipin, announced the target on Friday in Abuja at a press conference on implementing the Nigeria First Policy in the automotive sector. He said the plan would be phased, with local production rising from under 8 per cent to 20 per cent, then 40 per cent, and eventually 70 per cent of domestic demand.
NADDC Assemblers Shift To Completely Knocked Down Production
Osanipin said Nigeria's assembly capacity is estimated at between 400,000 and 500,000 units a year, with plants operated by PAN Nigeria, Innoson Vehicle Manufacturing and CIG Motors. Some manufacturers can produce tens of thousands of vehicles annually, he said, but need higher patronage to expand and bring down costs. Assemblers will be expected to move from semi-knocked-down (SKD) assembly to completely knocked-down (CKD) production, which requires more local input and component manufacturing.
He said NADDC will monitor manufacturers' investments, employment, production growth and delivery standards to ensure government patronage benefits the wider industry. He added that component makers could gain most, since vehicles need maintenance and replacement parts throughout their lifespan. He also said Nigeria must build local content to meet African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) rules of origin, which require 40 per cent local components for preferential access.
The director-general of the Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP), Adebowale Adedokun, said all federal entities have been directed to prioritise Nigerian-assembled vehicles. He said the policy has already cut prices, citing a model listed at over N70 million that his office bought for about N35 million after negotiation, with further discounts offered for additional units. Under the framework, federal ministries, departments and agencies must submit monthly and quarterly procurement reports to the BPP, which will report violations to the Presidency.
Government Sanctions Vehicle Suppliers For Procurement Violations
Manufacturers that breach the guidelines could be sanctioned or barred from supplying federal institutions. Adedokun said the EFCC and ICPC are also seeking procurement information, and that payments for vehicle purchases will be checked against BPP no-objection approvals. The chairman of the Nigerian Automotive Manufacturers Association, Bawo Omagbitse, said the policy reduces investment risk by giving manufacturers a more predictable market.
The national coordinator of the Automotive Local Component Manufacturers Association of Nigeria, Anslem Ilekuba, said a technology transfer programme has drawn interest from about 3,500 Chinese manufacturers. He said the association is also building a digital platform to link buyers with local component makers and improve parts traceability.

The rebound in foreign portfolio investment allowed the Central Bank of Egypt (CBE) to purchase foreign currency from the domestic market, contributing to a record $54.5 billion in international reserve assets in September, according to S&P.
Meanwhile, the banking system’s net foreign assets climbed to $31.2 billion, their highest level in six years.
The agency considers this positive net foreign asset position an important safeguard against external financial pressures, providing additional capacity to absorb potential capital outflows without immediately affecting central bank reserves.
Regional tensions and energy costs remain key risks
S&P anticipates that disruptions across the Middle East will continue into 2027, potentially keeping regional oil and gas supplies below their pre-conflict levels through the end of that year.
Against this backdrop, Egypt has sought to diversify its crude oil suppliers.
Saudi Arabia accounted for 66 percent of Egyptian oil imports in FY2025/2026, down from 89 percent in the preceding fiscal year.
S&P also noted that Egypt’s oil hedging arrangements offer partial protection against fluctuations in international energy prices.
The agency expects the current account deficit to reach approximately 5 percent of GDP in FY2026/2027, compared with 5.1 percent in FY2025/2026 and 4.2 percent in FY2024/2025.
The forecast reflects continued trade imbalances and higher energy import expenses, despite anticipated support from tourism, remittances, and Suez Canal receipts.
Inflation pressures complicate monetary easing
Egypt’s annual headline inflation reached 15.2 percent in March 2026 before moderating to 14.5 percent in August. This followed a 43-month low of 11.7 percent in September 2025.
The CBE had reduced interest rates by a combined 825 basis points between April 2025 and February 2026 before suspending further cuts amid renewed inflationary pressures from food and energy prices.
In September 2026, the central bank kept its overnight deposit and lending rates unchanged at 19 percent and 20 percent, respectively.
S&P forecasts average inflation of 12.9 percent in FY2026/2027, while warning that higher energy costs could push consumer prices above expectations.
The agency also expects yields on domestic government debt to decline more slowly, keeping debt-servicing expenses elevated.
Interest payments are projected to absorb approximately 60 percent of government revenues in FY2026/2027, compared with 68 percent in FY2025/2026, before declining further to 53 percent in FY2027/2028.
Over a broader horizon, S&P expects inflation to average approximately 12 percent across FY2026/2027 and FY2027/2028, before easing toward 9 percent in FY2028/2029.
Egypt’s economic growth expected to moderate to 4.5 percent
Egypt’s real GDP expanded by an estimated 5.1 percent in FY2025/2026, its strongest performance in three years, according to S&P.
The agency expects growth to ease to 4.5 percent in FY2026/2027.
Expansion in non-oil manufacturing, wholesale and retail activity, information and communications technology, and tourism contributed to the previous fiscal year’s economic performance.
Household spending also benefited from increased remittances, relatively lower inflation, and stable employment conditions.
Looking ahead, S&P expects exchange rate flexibility and structural reforms to support Egypt’s economic competitiveness.
However, the agency stressed that sustained growth will depend on stronger private-sector participation, improved governance, and further reductions in barriers to competition.
Additional priorities include bringing more informal economic activity into the formal sector, enhancing transparency and financial reporting among state-owned enterprises, and improving the competitive environment.
The government has already taken steps to improve resource allocation, including ending subsidized central bank lending programs for state-owned companies and tightening oversight of import-intensive public investment projects.
State asset sales could generate $1.5 billion by December
Egypt aims to raise an additional $1.5 billion through its state divestment program by December 2026.
Among the planned transactions is the sale of the government’s entire stake in the Gabal El-Zeit wind farm for $420 million.
The authorities are also targeting $106 million from partial disposals of the Finance Ministry’s holdings in publicly listed state-owned businesses.
Other anticipated transactions involve Banque du Caire and Misr Life Insurance, with proceeds expected to contribute to public debt reduction.
These planned sales follow approximately $2.2 billion generated from divestments in 2022 and 2023, alongside a $3.5 billion Qatari real estate investment agreement concluded in late 2025.
S&P considers progress in state asset divestments important for improving public finances, strengthening investor confidence, and expanding opportunities for private capital.
IMF and international partners provide financial support
Egypt’s IMF financing arrangement was expanded to $8 billion in March 2024, with the program later extended until December 2026.
The IMF completed its seventh review in July 2026, unlocking a $1.7 billion financing installment.
A final tranche of another $1.7 billion is expected in December 2026.
S&P does not anticipate Egypt entering a new IMF financing agreement after the current arrangement expires, although it expects the authorities to maintain close engagement with the fund under a nationally directed reform program.
Egypt also continues to benefit from international financial assistance, including the European Union’s €7.4 billion support package for 2024–2028.
The EU commitment consists of €5 billion in macro-financial assistance and budget-support lending, €1.8 billion in guarantees designed to stimulate private investment, and €600 million in development grants.
Additional concessional funding is expected from the World Bank, African Development Bank, and Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.
Gulf investment remains central to Egypt’s financing outlook
S&P expects Gulf Cooperation Council countries to maintain their financial engagement with Egypt, given the country’s regional strategic significance and its involvement in facilitating humanitarian assistance to Gaza.
However, the nature of Gulf financial support has shifted increasingly toward direct investment in projects and assets rather than deposits or unconditional assistance.
A prominent example is Abu Dhabi-based ADQ’s $35 billion investment commitment to the Ras El Hekma development in early 2024.
Egypt also reached an agreement with Qatar in November 2025 for a $30 billion development project in the Alam El Roum area along the North Coast, with implementation planned over seven years.
According to S&P, these large-scale investments should help reinforce foreign currency availability while supporting economic activity and private-sector development.
Budget deficit narrows as debt reduction efforts continue
Fiscal consolidation helped Egypt lower its overall budget deficit to 5.8 percent of GDP in FY2025/2026, alongside a primary surplus of 4.9 percent, according to S&P.
